blocks.text: 2.1.2 Creating Objects and Using Constructors in Java

One release of the alerting service brought three tickets. The subscriptions endpoint fails with `NoSuchMethodException: Subscription.<init>()`, although nobody removed a constructor. Rules created with the short constructor accept a negative limit, or never match their metric. An alert whose constructor threw an exception keeps logging `ALERT null`. Unit 2.1.1 covers the order in which initializers run, and an override called from a superclass constructor.
Declaring Any Constructor Takes Away the Default One
A class that declares no constructor gets a *default constructor*: no parameters, the class's own access, and a body that only calls `super()`. Someone added one constructor to `Subscription`:
JPA providers, and JSON mappers by default, build objects through the no-argument constructor:
Subscription s = Subscription.class.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
java.lang.NoSuchMethodException: Subscription.<init>()

Declaring a constructor removes the default one. javac doesn't check reflective calls, so the failure waited for the first request. A subclass with no constructor of its own stops compiling, because its default constructor calls `super()`:
error: constructor Subscription in class Subscription cannot be applied to given types;
A class that must be built both ways declares the no-argument constructor itself.
Overloaded Constructors Chain with this(...) to One That Checks and Assigns
The rule class had one constructor that checks its arguments. A two-argument one was added later, with the assignments copied:
Pause here: what does `new AlertRule(" CPU", -1)` build?

copied:  AlertRule[ CPU > -1.0 over PT5M]
chained: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: limit must be positive: -1.0

The copied constructor skipped the check and the normalisation. A limit of -1 is below every reading, and a rule for `" CPU"` never matches the `cpu` readings. `ChainedRule` is the same class with its short constructor delegating:
Every overload then ends in the one constructor that checks and assigns, and a check added there covers them all.

A `this(...)` or `super(...)` call must be the first statement. Parsing a spec such as `"cpu>90"` before delegating fails with `call to this must be first statement in constructor`. The arguments can't read instance fields either: `this(defaultLimit)` fails with `cannot reference defaultLimit before supertype constructor has been called`. Compute arguments with static methods inside the call:
chained: ChainedRule[cpu > 90.0 over PT5M]
Unit 2.1.1 shows what Java 25 relaxes.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Constructor That Hands Out this Lets Others Use a Half-Built Object

The price feed sends each new subscriber the last price at once. An alert, whose `symbol` and `limit` fields are `final` and whose `onPrice` prints an alert above `limit`, subscribes itself in its constructor:
The last price was 101.5. We create an alert at 120, then one at -5, then publish 102.0:

new PriceAlert(feed, "ACME", 120):
  ALERT null at 101.5
new PriceAlert(feed, "ACME", -5):
  ALERT null at 101.5
  limit must be positive: -5.0
listeners: 2; publish(102.0):
  ALERT null at 102.0

The feed called `onPrice` before the fields were assigned, so it read `null` and `0.0`, even though both are `final`. The second constructor threw and `new` returned nothing, but the feed already held the object. It answers every price for as long as the feed lives. The feed holds a reference, not a copy: on the same thread, every field the constructor assigned before throwing shows through it.
Moving `subscribe` to the last line helps only until a subclass adds fields (unit 2.1.1). Build the object first, and publish it from a static factory:

SafeAlert.watch(feed, "ACME", 120), then (feed, "ACME", -5):
  limit must be positive: -5.0
listeners: 1; publish(102.0):
Nothing fires: 102.0 is under 120, and the -5 alert was never subscribed. The private constructor forces every caller through `watch`.

**Threads.** The Java Language Specification (§17.5) promises that another thread sees a `final` field's assigned value if it got the reference after the constructor finished. A thread started in the constructor, or a listener registered there and called from another thread, can see fields assigned after that point at their defaults.
<!-- practice 2 -->
A Static Factory Can Name, Reuse or Choose the Class of What It Returns

Constructors are told apart only by their parameter types, so `Temperature(double celsius)` and `Temperature(double fahrenheit)` can't both exist: `constructor Temperature(double) is already defined`. Factories have names:
`new` always returns a new object of exactly the named class (an anonymous `new C() { }` aside). A factory may return an existing one, or a subclass:

same Currency: true
java.util.ImmutableCollections$List12
java.util.ImmutableCollections$ListN

`Currency` promises one instance per currency; `List.of` promises only an unmodifiable `List`. `==` compares references (unit 1.1.2), so it is true only when a factory returns the same object. Code that locks on a factory's result may share the lock with every other caller. Code that checks `getClass()` breaks when the JDK picks another class. Rely on identity or class only where the javadoc promises it: `Integer.valueOf` promises its cache only for -128 to 127 (unit 1.1.1).
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **Declaring any constructor takes away the default one.** Reflective frameworks then fail at run time, and subclasses stop compiling.
**Overloaded constructors chain with `this(...)` to one that checks and assigns.** A copied overload skips the checks; arguments are computed by static methods, since the call comes first.
**A constructor that hands out `this` lets others use a half-built object.** They see default values, and a constructor that throws leaves its escaped object behind. Publish from a factory.
**A static factory can name, reuse or choose the class of what it returns.** Callers rely on identity or class only where it is documented.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Your entity needs a no-argument constructor for JPA, but every object built in your own code must be valid. How do you keep application code off that constructor?
A base class registers `this` with a scheduler in its constructor. What can a subclass do about it, and what would you change in the base class?
Find a factory in a library you use that returns cached objects. Does its javadoc promise it?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why a Constructor Can't Choose What It Returns

`new` allocates the object before any constructor code runs, so a constructor can only fill in the object it was given. It can't return a cached one, pick a subclass, or have a name. That keeps `new` predictable. The cost is that every class needing more adds a static factory, and the reader no longer sees from the call whether the object is new.
